Introduction

Starting a Home Services Agency in Illinois allows you to provide non-medical personal care and homemaker services to individuals in their homes. Illinois has a large and growing senior population creating strong demand for quality home services.

The IL Department of Public Health (IDPH) oversees the licensing of Home Services Agencies under the Home Health, Home Services, and Home Nursing Agency Licensing Act.

With over 2.5 million residents aged 60 and older, Illinois presents significant opportunities for home services providers, particularly in the Chicago metropolitan area and underserved rural communities.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Illinois’s Regulations

  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Community Outreach
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Inspections
  • Frequently Asked Questions

1. Understand Illinois’s Regulations

IDPH licenses Home Services Agencies separately from Home Health Agencies. Key requirements:

  • State licensing through IDPH
  • Background checks via the Health Care Worker Background Check Act
  • Training requirements for home services workers
  • Service documentation standards
  • Quality monitoring and complaint investigation procedures

2. Choose the Type and Size of Agency

Service categories:

  • Personal care: Bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting assistance
  • Homemaker services: Cleaning, cooking, laundry, shopping
  • Companion services: Socialization and supervision
  • Respite care: Temporary relief for family caregivers

3. Business Structure and Licensing

  • Register with the IL Secretary of State
  • Obtain an EIN from the IRS
  • Apply for Home Services Agency license through IDPH
  • Complete Health Care Worker Background Check registration
  • Secure required insurance coverage

4. Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

Illinois financial benchmarks:

  • Private pay rates: $22 to $32 per hour
  • Medicaid rates: $18 to $24 per hour via Home Services Program
  • Break-even timeline: 12 to 18 months

5. Establish Operations Infrastructure

Set up office space, scheduling and billing systems, communication tools, and electronic documentation systems.

6. Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Illinois requires all home services workers to pass background checks and complete required training before providing services.

7. Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Develop policies for intake, care planning, incident reporting, employee management, and regulatory compliance.

8. Marketing and Community Outreach

Partner with hospitals, physicians, Area Agencies on Aging, and community organizations. Illinois’s Community Care Program is a significant referral source.

9. Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Inspections

Maintain licensing, conduct quality reviews, keep current training records, and stay updated on IDPH regulatory changes.

10. Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between Home Health and Home Services? Home Health provides medical services; Home Services provides non-medical personal care and homemaker services.

How do I bill the state program? Enroll as a provider through the Illinois Department on Aging’s Community Care Program.
